VBO:0200007.summary: Across southern African villages, Africanis dogs have long lived close to households and livestock, helping bring cattle from grazing and watching the homestead. This landrace was shaped by local work and conditions over generations, so its strengths and habits have room to vary from community to community.

sources.title: AfriCanis Society: What is in the name AfriCanis?
sources.evidence: Africanis Society describes the landrace's long association with southern African communities, cattle herding, homestead protection and local variation.

VBO:0200007.interestingFact: The name AfriCanis joins 'Africa' and 'Canis,' acknowledging the dogs' place in the continent's living heritage.

VBO:0200009.summary: Quiet watchfulness and independent judgment are central to the Akbash's character. It tends to be steady around its own flock, yet able to respond swiftly when a threat appears; generations of guarding sheep in western Turkey made that shift from calm observation to decisive action a practical skill.

sources.title: UKC Akbash Dog standard
sources.evidence: UKC standard identifies western Turkish flock-guarding, independent decision-making, calm watchfulness and speed/agility in confronting predators.

VBO:0200017.summary: Alaskan Malamutes are often playful and friendly with people, yet they can carry themselves with quiet dignity as adults. They were shaped to haul heavy loads across Arctic country, where strength, stamina and cooperation mattered more than racing speed; their sociability belongs beside a serious working past.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 243: Alaskan Malamute
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes sled-hauling strength and endurance over speed, an affectionate friendly temperament, playfulness and dignified maturity.

VBO:0200045.summary: The American English Coonhound is often sociable with people and other dogs, but a trail can reveal a remarkably persistent hunter. Bred for long nights after raccoon, it follows scent through woodland and uses its voice to keep hunters informed when the dog disappears from view.

sources.title: AKC American English Coonhound standard
sources.evidence: AKC coonhound standard describes an all-night hunting build, speed and endurance, sociability with people and dogs, and avid hunting.

VBO:0200049.summary: Alert, curious and energetic, the American Hairless Terrier still shows the keen instincts of its ratting-terrier ancestors. Its exposed skin makes traditional vermin work impractical, so that drive often finds other outlets in activity and sport; it remains a lively dog engaged with the people around it.
VBO:0200049.historicalRoots: American Rat Terrier-derived companion and sport terrier.

sources.title: AKC American Hairless Terrier standard
sources.evidence: AKC standard identifies ratting ancestry, retained hunting instinct, hairless variety's limits in hunting, activity/sports aptitude, and alert curious energetic temperament.

VBO:0200062.summary: Composed and watchful, an Anatolian Shepherd Dog may make its own judgment when livestock face a threat. Its independent character reflects long days guarding animals across Turkey's pastoral country, where a dog needed the endurance to range with a flock and the nerve to act when its handler was far away.

sources.title: AKC Anatolian Shepherd Dog standard
sources.evidence: AKC standard identifies Anatolian livestock-guardian purpose, large but agile enduring build, composed temperament and protective independence.

VBO:0200090.summary: Kelpies are typically alert, eager to work and quick to read the movement of sheep. On the huge runs of New South Wales and Victoria they learned to gather and drive stock through heat and dust, working both open country and yards with a strong instinct for where a flock needs to go.
VBO:0200090.historicalRoots: Australian sheepdog developed from Scottish collie-type imports.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 293: Australian Kelpie
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents vast Australian sheep properties and difficult climate, plus alert eager disposition and instinct for sheep work in open country and yards.

VBO:0200090.interestingFact: The breed's early stock drew on collie-type dogs imported from Scotland, then adapted to Australian conditions.

VBO:0200098.summary: The Australian Terrier is often lively, persistent and loyal, with an even nature that helped it live closely with people. It was bred as a small helper in rough Australian country, taking on practical terrier work around farms while remaining a companion when the day's jobs were done.
VBO:0200098.historicalRoots: Australian working terrier shaped from British imports.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 8: Australian Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard details Australian rough-terrain helper role, British terrier ancestry, working character, loyalty and even disposition.

VBO:0200110.summary: In Jammu and Kashmir, Bakharwal dogs accompany Bakarwal and Gujjar flocks into high pastures during seasonal movement. They have been kept to watch sheep and goats against wild predators, a job that places the dog alongside pastoral families for long stretches of mountain travel.
VBO:0200110.historicalRoots: Jammu and Kashmir pastoral livestock guardian.

sources.title: Indian Journal of Tropical Biodiversity: Bakerwal dog survey
sources.evidence: Primary Bakerwal field survey identifies the Bakarwal and Gujjar communities, highland migration with small ruminants, and protection against predators.

VBO:0200124.summary: Lively and affectionate away from a hunt, the Basset Bleu de Gascogne can become single-minded on rabbit or hare scent. It may work alone or with a pack, following a trail with a fine nose and resonant voice; western French hunters revived the breed in the late nineteenth century.
VBO:0200124.historicalRoots: French rabbit-and-hare scent hound revived in the late nineteenth century.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 35: Basset Bleu de Gascogne
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents rabbit/hare work alone or in packs, scent and howling voice, lively affectionate temperament, and late-nineteenth-century revival.

VBO:0200131.summary: A Beagle is typically merry and even-tempered, but hare scent can bring out a pack hunter's remarkable persistence. Its steady pace once let hunters follow on foot; Tudor-era records even mention wirehaired and tiny 'pocket' Beagles, surprising branches in this familiar hound's history.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 161: Beagle
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives hare hunting on foot, pack work, stamina and determination, merry even temperament, and Tudor-era wirehaired and pocket Beagles.

VBO:0200137.summary: The Bedlington Terrier can be affectionate and mild in repose, then spirited and courageous when a sporting instinct wakes up. Its Rothbury ancestors came from northern England's mining districts, where small terriers helped put rabbits on the table; that contrast between gentleness and grit is part of the breed's appeal.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 9: Bedlington Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard traces Rothbury mining-district rabbit work and describes a mild resting expression, confidence, affection, sporting instinct and courage.

VBO:0200161.summary: Bernese Mountain Dogs are generally attentive, steady and good-natured with familiar people. On farms around Bern they watched the property, moved cattle and pulled loads, shifting between jobs in a working day; the older name Dürrbächler remembers a hamlet where these versatile farm dogs were common.
VBO:0200161.historicalRoots: Bernese farm guard, draught and cattle dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 45: Bernese Mountain Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard records Bernese farm guard/draught/cattle work, attentive placid and devoted temperament, and the Dürrbach naming history.

VBO:0200174.summary: The Black Russian Terrier is often composed and responsive, yet can move quickly into a defensive response when needed and settle again afterward. It was deliberately developed in Russia for service and guarding, where intelligence, endurance and controlled courage mattered more than the 'terrier' name suggests.
VBO:0200174.historicalRoots: Twentieth-century Russian guard and service dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 327: Black Russian Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard details deliberate Russian guard/service development and a controlled temperament that activates defensively then settles, with endurance and trainability.

VBO:0200189.summary: The Bolognese tends to be calm and closely attached to familiar people, a dog whose long job has been companionship. European courts prized it as a gift, and paintings by Titian, Bruegel and Goya preserve that history; its quiet social attentiveness grew in rooms rather than fields.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 196: Bolognese
sources.evidence: FCI standard recounts Italian court gifts and portraits by named artists, and describes a serene, generally low-activity dog faithful to familiar people.

VBO:0200197.summary: A Borzoi may seem calm with people while remaining keenly responsive to movement. In Russian hunting country it searched for hare and fox at a measured pace, then launched into a gallop when game appeared; wolves were part of the breed's history too, though less common quarry.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 193: Borzoi
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives Russian hare/fox pursuit and less frequent wolf hunting, describes slow search changing to full gallop, calm temperament and visual responsiveness.

VBO:0200210.summary: Boxers are often playful and engaging with their household, yet watchful when something seems wrong. Their older Brabant Bullenbeisser ancestors held game until hunters arrived; the modern breed combines that courageous background with an even, sociable manner in familiar company.
VBO:0200210.historicalRoots: German Bullenbeisser-descended hunting and working dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 144: Boxer
sources.evidence: FCI standard explains Bullenbeisser game-holding ancestry and describes household loyalty, friendly play, watchfulness, courage and even temperament.

VBO:0200232.summary: Brazilian Trackers are described as calm and balanced away from a trail, but persistent hunters when scent takes over. Selected from American Foxhound stock, they can flush and corner game alone or with other dogs; breeders rebuilt the line after a severe twentieth-century decline.
VBO:0200232.historicalRoots: Brazilian foxhound-derived tracking and hunting breed.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 275: Brazilian Tracker
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes Brazilian selection from American Foxhounds, flushing/cornering work, solo or group hunts, calm balanced temperament and post-decline revival.

VBO:0200255.summary: Bull Terriers can be playful, friendly and sometimes stubborn, with an even disposition prized alongside their courage. James Hinks established the recognizable breed in the 1850s; its sociable, mischievous character has remained as distinctive as the look that first made it famous.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 11: Bull Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard credits Hinks with 1850s standardization and describes courage, fun-loving spirit, occasional obstinacy, even temperament and friendliness to people.

VBO:0200267.summary: Cairn Terriers are typically active and cheerful, with fearlessness and self-possession that can emerge on a task. Their ancestors pursued vermin among the stone and brush of Scotland's Western Highlands and Isle of Skye, where a small dog had to keep investigating even after quarry disappeared into a cairn.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 4: Cairn Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes active hardy fearless but nonaggressive temperament; Royal Kennel Club traces Scottish Highland/Skye vermin work.

sources.title: Royal Kennel Club: Cairn Terrier
sources.evidence: Places the breed in the Scottish Western Highlands and Isle of Skye, where it worked vermin among rocky cairns.

VBO:0200273.summary: Watchful and accustomed to close farm life, the Can de Palleiro helped Galician families both drive livestock and guard animals or property. Its name recalls the hayloft where these dogs often slept, a small detail that places this working companion inside the daily routine of rural Galicia.

sources.title: Xunta de Galicia: Can de Palleiro
sources.evidence: Xunta de Galicia breed account explains the hayloft name and traditional Galician farm use, including livestock driving and guarding.

VBO:0200299.summary: Catalan Sheepdogs are often vigilant, hardy and devoted to their shepherd, while willing to use their own initiative. In the Pyrenees they moved flocks and corrected straying animals through heat, cold and changeable weather; the job rewarded a dog that stayed attentive without waiting for every cue.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 87: Catalan Sheepdog
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Catalan Pyrenean flock driving, initiative with straying animals, vigilance, hardiness in varied weather and devotion to shepherd and flock.

VBO:0200321.summary: Quiet self-assurance and independent judgment are hallmarks of the Central Asian Shepherd Dog. Across a vast region it guarded herds, caravans and homes, conserving energy until a large predator or other threat required action; its territorial watchfulness grew from that demanding work.
VBO:0200321.historicalRoots: Central Asian herd, caravan and homestead guardian.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 335: Central Asian Shepherd Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes Central Asian herd/caravan/home protection, harsh conditions, calm independent territorial temperament and courage toward predators.

VBO:0200344.summary: The Chinese Chongqing Dog is often calm and affectionate with its own family, yet alert and somewhat aloof with strangers. In southwestern China it was kept for scent-led hunting and home protection, work that called for courage and close attention to unfamiliar activity around the household.
VBO:0200344.historicalRoots: Southwestern Chinese hunting and guarding tradition.

sources.title: Chongqing Pet Association breed standard
sources.evidence: Chongqing breed association describes the breed's local hunting and home-protection history; its standard describes alertness, courage and loyalty.

sources.title: Chinese Chongqing Dog — Breed Info
sources.evidence: Breed association identifies Chongqing origin and historical scent hunting and home protection.

sources.title: Chinese Chongqing Dog — Temperament
sources.evidence: Breed association describes a calm, confident, alert dog, affectionate with family and somewhat aloof with strangers.

VBO:0200354.summary: Chippiparai dogs observed around Tirunelveli were affectionate with familiar people but alert to strangers, alongside a strong local hunting tradition. This Tamil Nadu sighthound pursues hare by sight and speed; surveyed owners described taking their dogs into nearby forest for regular hare hunts.

sources.title: Indian Journal of Veterinary Sciences and Biotechnology: Chippiparai field study
sources.evidence: Primary veterinary field study locates the Tirunelveli home tract, records local hare hunts, speed and stamina, and reports owner observations of affection at home and alertness toward strangers.

VBO:0200365.summary: The Cirneco dell'Etna can be resolute and strong-willed in a chase, yet affectionate with familiar people. On Sicily's rocky slopes it uses scent to find wild rabbit in crevices, a precise hunting skill with deep local roots; dogs like it appear on ancient coins from the island.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 199: Cirneco dell'Etna
sources.evidence: FCI standard specifies rocky Etna rabbit hunting by scent, resolute strong-willed and affectionate temperament, and ancient Sicilian depictions.

VBO:0200397.summary: The Curly Coated Retriever is often steady, confident and friendly with people it knows, though it may seem reserved at first. Bred for British game retrieval, it can work independently through difficult cover; that self-reliant streak distinguishes its style from a more exuberant retriever's.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 110: Curly Coated Retriever
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies British retrieving use and describes steady, reliable, bold, friendly, self-confident, independent temperament that may appear aloof.

VBO:0200429.summary: The Dandie Dinmont Terrier is a determined, persistent worker with a sensitive and affectionate side. It can show an independent sporting streak, then settle into a dignified gentleness with its people; its unusual name came from a terrier-keeping character in Sir Walter Scott’s novel Guy Mannering.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 168: Dandie Dinmont Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes a game, independent, determined and persistent terrier that is also sensitive, affectionate and dignified.

sources.title: Royal Kennel Club: Dandie Dinmont Terrier
sources.evidence: Royal Kennel Club traces the breed’s name to the terrier-keeping character in Sir Walter Scott’s novel Guy Mannering.

VBO:0200445.summary: Courageous and steady under pressure, the Dogo Argentino was bred for big-game hunting in Córdoba. It follows scent across difficult ground and tends to stay quiet on the trail; its breeding tradition also prizes restraint toward people, distinguishing hunting nerve from indiscriminate hostility.
VBO:0200445.historicalRoots: Córdoba big-game hunting dog developed in the twentieth century.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 292: Dogo Argentino
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Antonio Nores Martínez's Córdoba breeding project for big-game hunting and describes scenting ability, courage, quiet trailing and a nonaggressive attitude toward people.

VBO:0200453.summary: The Drentsche Patrijshond is an attentive partner that tends to keep track of its hunter instead of ranging far away. It searches for birds, points and retrieves; as scent strengthens, its tail may make small circles before the dog freezes into a point, a revealing moment in its cooperative field style.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 224: Drentsche Patrijshond
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes close cooperative hunting, pointing, retrieving, attention to the hunter and characteristic tail circling when taking game scent.

VBO:0200463.summary: Alert, independent and persistent, the Dutch Shepherd could work with a shepherd yet make decisions without one. It once served as a living fence along crop edges, keeping sheep off the fields, and also moved flocks to market; that mix of initiative and cooperation remains central to its character.
VBO:0200463.historicalRoots: Dutch sheep and farm-boundary working dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 223: Dutch Shepherd
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes the moving-fence role, market flock driving and other farm work, plus loyal, alert, active, independent and persistent temperament.

VBO:0200495.summary: The English Setter is often intensely friendly with people while remaining active and keen for game. In the field it searches for birds and holds a point so the hunter can approach; its open social manner and focused working drive are both longstanding parts of the breed's identity.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 2: English Setter
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies the breed as a bird-finding pointing dog and describes keen game sense, activity and an intensely friendly temperament.

VBO:0200508.summary: The Estonian Hound is generally friendly and even-tempered, with agility that serves it well when following a scent. It was shaped for difficult forest country, where a resonant voice helps hunters locate a dog out of sight; its development also sought a smaller local hound suited to Estonian conditions.
VBO:0200508.historicalRoots: Estonian hare, fox and lynx hound standardized in 1954.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 366: Estonian Hound
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes scent work over difficult terrain, a resonant voice, agile friendly even temperament and deliberate Estonian development of a smaller hound.

VBO:0200519.summary: Field Spaniels are often notably docile and sensitive, yet capable of independent decisions while working. A rough-shooting hunter relies on one to search cover, flush game and retrieve it; the breed's practical character survived two severe declines through deliberate efforts to rebuild it.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 123: Field Spaniel
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents rough-shooting flushing/retrieving use, docile sensitive active independent temperament and two periods when the breed nearly vanished.

VBO:0200528.summary: Optimism is a memorable Flat-Coated Retriever trait: the breed is usually friendly, confident and ready for another job. It was shaped for retrieving shot game, including birds and hare, so its buoyant manner sits alongside the stamina and purpose needed for a long day afield.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 121: Flat-Coated Retriever
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies natural gundog retrieving work, including carrying hare or pheasant, and describes confident, kindly, optimistic and friendly temperament.

VBO:0200550.summary: The French Water Dog, or Barbet, is often sociable and closely attached to its handler, with a particular eagerness for water. It searches marshy vegetation, flushes birds and retrieves them even in cold conditions; that affinity for wet work is a living part of its temperament and history.
VBO:0200550.historicalRoots: French waterfowl flushing and retrieving dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 105: French Water Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard details waterfowl searching, flushing and retrieving in aquatic vegetation and cold water, and describes an even, sociable dog attached to its handler.

VBO:0201454.summary: The German Pinscher is typically lively, intelligent and self-assured, with the evenness to stay engaged through a day's activity. It carries an old farm-watchdog tradition; early smooth Pinschers and rough-coated Schnauzers came from the same stock, before their paths separated.
VBO:0201454.historicalRoots: German smooth-coated watch and companion dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 184: German Pinscher
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes watchdog use, lively spirited intelligent self-assured even temperament and the common early stock of smooth Pinschers and rough Schnauzers.

VBO:0200602.summary: Steady nerves and self-control around gunfire are prized in the German Wirehaired Pointer. It moves between searching, pointing and retrieving in field, forest and water, both before and after a shot; the versatile work asks for focus that holds when the surroundings change.
VBO:0200602.historicalRoots: German all-terrain pointing and retrieving gundog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 98: German Wirehaired Pointer
sources.evidence: FCI standard specifies versatile field/forest/water hunting before and after the shot and a firm, self-controlled, balanced temperament without shyness around gunfire.

VBO:0200613.summary: A Gordon Setter is often bold, outgoing and kindly, as well as alert to game. It searches for birds and holds a point for a hunter; the breed's association with the Duke of Gordon's Scottish kennels gives this active sporting dog a particularly vivid chapter in setter history.

sources.title: Royal Kennel Club: Gordon Setter
sources.evidence: Royal Kennel Club account traces the breed to the Duke of Gordon’s Scottish kennels and its sporting background.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 6: Gordon Setter
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies pointing work and bold, outgoing, intelligent, kindly, even temperament.

VBO:0200631.summary: Greater Swiss Mountain Dogs tend to be self-confident and watchful, devoted to familiar people while measured with strangers. Swiss farms used them to move cattle, guard property and pull loads; a 1908 exhibition helped bring surviving examples of the old working type back to notice.
VBO:0200631.historicalRoots: Swiss watch, draught and droving dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 58: Greater Swiss Mountain Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents cattle driving, guarding and draught work, confident watchful temperament and Albert Heim's 1908 recognition of the surviving farm type.

VBO:0200655.summary: Friendly and even-tempered away from the hunt, the Hamiltonstövare becomes a determined solo scent hound after hare or fox. Its voice announces the trail rather than a pack's progress; the breed took its name from Count Adolf Patrick Hamilton, an influential figure in Swedish hound breeding.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 132: Hamiltonstovare
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives solo hare/fox hunting with voice, friendly even temperament and the naming history of Count Hamilton.

VBO:0200671.summary: The Hokkaido is typically faithful and alert, with boldness in work and a docile response to its handler. Ainu hunters used these dogs to pursue bear in Japan's northern country, where endurance and judgment mattered; the breed later became one of Japan's designated natural monuments.
VBO:0200671.historicalRoots: Hokkaido hunting dog associated with Ainu communities.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 261: Hokkaido
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes Ainu bear-hunting history, stamina, alert bold temperament, faithfulness and docility, and natural-monument designation.

VBO:0200683.summary: A Huntaway moves New Zealand sheep with its voice, using a deep, repeated bark to drive a flock through yards or over hills. Farmers have selected for working ability rather than one fixed look; the skill to control stock at a distance makes this dog a distinct partner in the country's large-scale sheep farming.
VBO:0200683.historicalRoots: New Zealand voiced sheep-driving working dog.

sources.title: Te Ara: Farm dogs
sources.evidence: Te Ara's New Zealand farm-dog account describes the Huntaway's deep barking drive of sheep in yards and hill country and selection for work over uniform type.

VBO:0200695.summary: INDogs are indigenous village dogs shaped by generations of life alongside Indian communities. In rural settings they may help move cattle and watch homesteads, while free-ranging life rewards close attention to people, animals and local conditions; the name covers a living landrace rather than a single kennel line.

sources.title: INDog Project: indigenous village dog
sources.evidence: INDog Project describes the indigenous village-dog landrace, rural free-ranging life, cattle herding and homestead watching, and variation across local populations.

VBO:0200705.summary: The Irish Water Spaniel is often eager, bold and enduring, yet can be discerning with strangers and playful with familiar people. It comes from wildfowling, searching heavy cover and retrieving birds from water; its loyalty and humor add a lively household side to a demanding sporting past.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 124: Irish Water Spaniel
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies wildfowling, heavy-cover and water retrieving, plus eager bold stamina-rich temperament, loyalty, humor and discernment with strangers.

VBO:0200710.summary: Gentle and even-tempered with familiar people, the Istrian Wire-Haired Hound can be persistent once a scent takes hold. It follows hare, fox and sometimes wild boar over stony hills, using its voice to keep hunters in touch; rough weather has long been part of its working country.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 152: Istrian Wire-Haired Hound
sources.evidence: FCI standard specifies hare/fox/boar scent hunting in stony terrain and varied weather, vocal tracking, trainability, devotion and gentle even temperament.

VBO:0200724.summary: The Jack Russell Terrier is often lively, fearless and friendly, with confidence that makes sense in an earth-working hunter. Descended from Reverend John Russell's fox dogs, it pursues quarry above ground and can follow it below; Australian breeders continued shaping that spirited working line.
VBO:0200724.historicalRoots: English fox-terrier line developed further in Australia.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 345: Jack Russell Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard traces Reverend Russell's fox terriers and Australian development, describes above- and below-ground fox work and lively alert bold friendly confident temperament.

VBO:0200735.summary: Clever and mild, the Japanese Chin was shaped by centuries of close companionship in aristocratic households. Tradition records dogs arriving from Korea in the eighth century, with later generations kept in Japanese courts; its long social role is quite distinct from that of a working terrier or hound.
VBO:0200735.historicalRoots: East Asian court companion developed in Japan.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 206: Japanese Chin
sources.evidence: FCI standard records early Korean diplomatic gifts, later Japanese court keeping and a clever, mild temperament.

VBO:0200747.summary: Keen and highly alert, the Kai Ken was shaped by hunting wild boar and deer in the steep mountains of Japan's Kai district. Its hunting heritage included work in packs, calling for stamina and attention to other dogs as well as quarry; Japan designated the breed a natural monument in 1934.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 317: Kai Ken
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes Kai mountain hunting of boar and deer, pack tendency, keen alert temperament and 1934 natural-monument designation.

VBO:0200754.summary: The Karelian Bear Dog is an eager, independent hunter that can still cooperate closely with a person. It pursues elk or bear, then marks stopped game with persistent barking; a keen nose and strong sense of direction help it stay oriented during a demanding chase through northern country.
VBO:0200754.historicalRoots: Karelian and Finnish big-game hunting spitz.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 48: Karelian Bear Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes independent but cooperative elk/bear hunting, barking to hold or mark game, keen scent, orientation and eager persistence.

VBO:0200764.summary: Keen and alert, the Kerry Blue Terrier retains the purposeful character of an Irish farm worker. It tackled vermin and could go underground after badger or otter; those demanding jobs help explain a determined streak that remains visible in its approach to a task.
VBO:0200764.historicalRoots: Irish all-round farm and sporting terrier.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 3: Kerry Blue Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard recounts Irish farm work, vermin control and otter/badger hunting and characterizes the breed as keen and alert with terrier character.

VBO:0200778.summary: Kombai dogs observed in Tamil Nadu’s Theni district showed watchfulness toward strangers and responsiveness to familiar handlers. Named for a local village, this regional type has been kept for guarding homes and property; its strongest recorded tradition is protection close to the household.

sources.title: Veterinary Practitioner: phenotypic characterization of Kombai dogs
sources.evidence: Primary 2023 veterinary field survey locates the Kombai in Theni, describes guarding use and records stranger wariness and obedience to owners among sampled dogs.

VBO:0200793.summary: Brave and self-confident, the Kuvasz was trusted to protect Hungarian flocks and property even when people were out of reach. Its devotion to a charge grew from that independent guardian role; the breed also appeared at the court of King Matthias Corvinus, where it could accompany hunts.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 54: Kuvasz
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes Hungarian flock/property guarding, brave fearless self-confident temperament and historical hunting use in King Matthias Corvinus's court.

VBO:0200816.summary: The Large Münsterländer is often lively without nervousness and readily taught, a temperament suited to close teamwork with a hunter. It searches field, forest and water, points game and retrieves after the shot; its distinct breed line endured after black dogs were excluded from another German pointing register.
VBO:0200816.historicalRoots: German versatile pointing and retrieving dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 118: Large Munsterlander
sources.evidence: FCI standard covers field/forest/water hunting, pre- and post-shot work, tractable reliable lively temperament, and the early black German Longhaired Pointer registration split.

VBO:0200836.summary: Affectionate and attentive, the Löwchen tends to watch people closely and can settle quietly when asked. European courts long kept it as a companion, and historical art preserves its presence there; its social responsiveness is the skill behind a breed whose working day unfolded beside people.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 233: Lowchen
sources.evidence: FCI standard recounts courtly companionship and historical depictions, and describes affectionate attentive receptive temperament with calm behavior on command.

VBO:0200865.summary: Perceptive and devoted to its charge, the Maremma Sheepdog has long guarded flocks in central Italy. Seasonal movement between the Abruzzo mountains and Maremma lowlands brought two regional working strains together; the dog had to stay alert to danger through the shepherd's long journeys.
VBO:0200865.historicalRoots: Italian Abruzzo and Maremma flock-protection dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 201: Maremma Sheepdog
sources.evidence: FCI standard explains flock protection, transhumance between Abruzzo and Maremma, merger of regional strains and perceptive devoted guardian temperament.

VBO:0200896.summary: Alert, intelligent and fearless, the Miniature Schnauzer tends to notice activity around a home and make its presence known. It grew from small rough-haired farm dogs of the Frankfurt region; the watchful temperament links that working ancestry to its long role as a close companion.
VBO:0200896.historicalRoots: German small rough-haired pinscher and Schnauzer tradition.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 183: Miniature Schnauzer
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes alert fearless intelligent enduring temperament, watch/companion use and origins among small rough-haired Pinschers near Frankfurt.

VBO:0200921.summary: The Mudi is often quick to learn, eager to work and courageous around difficult livestock. This Hungarian herder also took part in wild-boar drives and watched property, so its lively attention was useful across several rural jobs; it can switch from close stock control to sounding an alarm.
VBO:0200921.historicalRoots: Hungarian herding dog from local and prick-eared German stock.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 238: Mudi
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies difficult-stock herding, wild-boar battue and watch work, and describes quick learning, courage, lively temperament and keen work drive.

VBO:0200935.summary: The New Zealand Heading Dog controls sheep with movement and a fixed gaze, often circling wide before bringing a flock toward its handler. Unlike the barking Huntaway, it is selected to work quietly; farmers value that close, precise control for yard work such as separating sheep from a mob.
VBO:0200935.historicalRoots: New Zealand sheep-heading dog developed from Border Collies.

sources.title: Te Ara: Farm dogs
sources.evidence: Te Ara farm-dog account distinguishes quiet Heading Dogs from barking Huntaways and describes casting, eye-based sheep control and close yard work.

VBO:0200955.summary: The Norwegian Elkhound brings courage, stamina and quick judgment to moose hunting. It can track through rough northern country, then bark, dodge and circle to hold a much larger animal until a hunter arrives; that mix of persistence and agility is the skill behind its name.

sources.title: AKC Norwegian Elkhound standard
sources.evidence: AKC breed standard and breed history describe Norwegian moose hunting, tracking stamina and barking to hold quarry, with courage and agility around large game.

VBO:0000668.summary: Steady, quiet and determined, the Old Danish Pointing Dog hunts at a measured pace while staying in touch with its handler. It searches without needless commotion, and Danish tradition traces the line to Morten Bak's eighteenth-century breeding of local farm and traveling dogs.
VBO:0000668.historicalRoots: Danish bird-pointing dog founded near Glenstrup.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 281: Old Danish Pointing Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes quiet slow close-contact hunting, stable determined courageous temperament and Morten Bak's early Danish breeding history.

VBO:0200989.summary: Patagonian Sheepdogs were shaped by practical flock work in southern Chile after European sheepdogs reached the region. They still help manage sheep, and sometimes cattle, on widely separated farms; generations of selection and geographic isolation gave this regional working population a history distinct from its imported ancestors.

sources.title: Diversity: Patagonian Sheepdog historical perspective
sources.evidence: Primary peer-reviewed Patagonian Sheepdog study documents sheep and some cattle work, European sheepdog ancestry, late-nineteenth/early-twentieth-century introduction and geographic isolation.

VBO:0201016.summary: Alert and playful away from a hunt, the Pharaoh Hound is often affectionate with familiar people. In Malta it pursues small game by sight, scent and hearing, using its ears to locate quarry among rocky fields; the living island hunting practice gives the breed a story beyond its ancient-looking name.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 248: Pharaoh Hound
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Maltese small-game hunting by sight, scent and hearing, and describes alert intelligent friendly affectionate playful temperament.

VBO:0201035.summary: The Polish Lowland Sheepdog is often lively, vigilant and quick to remember what matters around a flock. It both moves sheep and watches over them, using close attention to the shepherd and surroundings; that perceptive character also fits the breed's traditional farm-guard role.
VBO:0201035.historicalRoots: Polish lowland herding and farm-watch dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 251: Polish Lowland Sheepdog
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives Polish flock-herding and guarding purpose and describes lively, vigilant, perceptive, intelligent temperament with good memory.

VBO:0201064.summary: The Porcelaine follows small-game scent through French hunting country and drives quarry toward hunters waiting ahead. It does a different job from a pointing dog: the chase must continue long enough for people to position themselves, and the hound's skill lies in keeping that moving trail alive.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 30: Porcelaine
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies the French Porcelaine as a scenthound used for small-game driving toward waiting guns.

VBO:0201077.summary: Portuguese Water Dogs are often intelligent and vigorous, with an independent streak that can shade into wilfulness. They worked beside fishermen, carrying messages between boats and retrieving gear from the water; a willingness to swim and dive made them especially useful along Portugal's Algarve coast.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 37: Portuguese Water Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents fishing assistance, swimming/diving and Algarve concentration, and describes intelligent, courageous, impetuous and wilful temperament.

VBO:0201105.summary: The Pumi is typically bold, busy and vocal, with some reserve toward strangers. Hungarian herders used it to turn larger livestock and sound an alarm around the farm; its early lines combined Puli-type dogs with imported terrier-like herders, helping explain its lively working style.
VBO:0201105.historicalRoots: Hungarian herder shaped from Puli and continental terrier types.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 56: Pumi
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes larger-stock herding, alert vocal temperament, boldness, activity, stranger reserve and Puli/terrier-like ancestry.

VBO:0201122.summary: The Rajapalayam comes from the area around its namesake town in southern Tamil Nadu. Local households have mainly kept these dogs to guard farms and farmhouses, where watching familiar ground and responding to unfamiliar activity are practical daily jobs; their history is closely tied to that farming region.
VBO:0201122.historicalRoots: Rajapalayam district, Tamil Nadu indigenous working dog.

sources.title: ICAR: phenotypic characterization of Rajapalayam
sources.evidence: Primary ICAR home-tract study locates the breed around Rajapalayam and records its main use guarding farms and farmhouses.

VBO:0201137.summary: The Lagotto Romagnolo is generally tractable, affectionate and keen to follow scent. It once retrieved birds from Romagna's marshes, but wetland drainage redirected its nose toward truffles hidden underground; that unusual change of quarry is one of the breed's most memorable skills.
VBO:0201137.historicalRoots: Romagna marsh retriever turned truffle-searching dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 298: Romagna Water Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents the shift from marsh water retrieval to truffle search after drainage, scent aptitude and tractable affectionate alert temperament.

VBO:0201160.summary: Saint Bernards are generally friendly and watchful, with individuals ranging from calm to lively. At the Great St Bernard Pass, monks kept them as guards and used them to find travelers lost in snow or fog; the famous rescue role grew from the daily needs of an actual mountain hospice.
VBO:0201160.historicalRoots: Great St. Bernard Pass hospice and alpine rescue dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 61: Saint Bernard
sources.evidence: FCI standard records hospice guard and traveler-rescue work in snow/fog at the Great St Bernard Pass and describes friendly watchful temperament from calm to lively.

VBO:0201181.summary: Lively, cheerful and watchful, the Schapendoes brings an independent mind to sheep work. On Dutch heathlands it needed quick turns, jumping ability and stamina to manage flocks; after nearly disappearing during the Second World War, the breed was rebuilt by dedicated keepers.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 313: Schapendoes
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes heathland sheep work, speed/jumping/endurance, intelligent watchful jolly friendly temperament and postwar recovery.

VBO:0201195.summary: The Scottish Deerhound is commonly gentle, friendly and dignified, with an eagerness to please that contrasts with its formidable chase. It was bred to course red deer across open Scottish country, a pursuit demanding speed and persistence; the partnership reaches back many centuries.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 164: Scottish Deerhound
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies red-deer coursing and describes gentle friendly dignified temperament, obedience and eagerness to please; historical section notes centuries of use.

VBO:0201207.summary: Lively and kind-natured, the Serbian Hound can become tenacious when it finds a trail. This Balkan scent hunter uses stamina and a clear voice to keep the chase moving; once called the Balkan Hound, it took its present name as the regional hunting tradition became more closely tied to Serbia.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 150: Serbian Hound
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Balkan scent-hunting history, clear voice and tenacity, describes lively kind dependable temperament and documents the renaming to Serbian Hound.

VBO:0201225.summary: Keen, energetic and highly alert, the Shikoku was shaped by boar hunting in Japan's Kochi mountains. It remains responsive to its handler while pursuing game over steep terrain; the old Awa, Hongawa and Hata lines preserve the breed's connection to different local hunting communities.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 319: Shikoku
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes Kochi mountain boar hunting, keen energetic alert temperament with handler docility and the Awa/Hongawa/Hata regional strains.

VBO:0201240.summary: The Skye Terrier often forms a strong bond with one person and may be reserved when strangers first approach. Its ancestors pursued quarry among the rocks and earth of Scotland's western islands; Greyfriars Bobby's famous vigil became a lasting story of the breed's devotion.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 75: Skye Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes western Scottish origin, terrier work, devotion to one person and reserve with strangers; breed history records Greyfriars Bobby.

VBO:0201296.summary: Staffordshire Bull Terriers tend to be affectionate and playful with familiar people, bringing a warm social manner to everyday life. They also retain the courage and tenacity of their terrier ancestry; an intelligent, watchful dog can shift from play to focused attention when something around it changes.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 76: Staffordshire Bull Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes Staffordshire Bull Terrier courage, tenacity, intelligence and affection.

sources.title: American Kennel Club: Get to Know the Bully Breeds
sources.evidence: AKC describes the Staffordshire Bull Terrier’s playful, loyal and sweet social character and its watchdog role.

VBO:0201316.summary: Alert, energetic and fearless, the Swedish Vallhund can work close to cattle heels with confidence around much larger animals. The breed survived on farms in West Gothland, where a 1940s search found remaining dogs and helped preserve an old Swedish herding tradition.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 14: Swedish Vallhund
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes Swedish cattle-heeling use, watchful energetic fearless alert temperament and the West Gothland rediscovery in the 1940s.

VBO:0201347.summary: The Thai Bangkaew Dog is often alert, intelligent and loyal, with some reserve toward strangers. Its name comes from a village in Phitsanulok, where watchful household dogs developed a local identity; readiness to learn and respond to familiar people complements that guarding instinct.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 358: Thai Bangkaew Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard traces the breed to Bangkaew village in Phitsanulok and describes alert intelligent loyal watchful temperament, trainability and stranger reserve.

VBO:0201353.summary: Lively and good-natured with familiar people, the Tibetan Terrier may be more reserved on a first meeting. It lived with Tibetan families, travelers and herders as a companion and watchful partner; despite the name, it is not a working earth terrier.
VBO:0201353.historicalRoots: Tibetan herding, travel and companion dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 209: Tibetan Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard states the breed is not a true terrier, recounts Tibetan companion and watch roles, and describes lively good-natured alert intelligent temperament with stranger reserve.

VBO:0201374.summary: Active, alert and intelligent, the Treeing Walker Coonhound can stay with a raccoon scent deep into a night hunt. It signals from the base of a tree when quarry is located, using its characteristic voice to guide a hunter to the end of a trail that may be out of sight.

sources.title: AKC Treeing Walker Coonhound standard
sources.evidence: AKC standard describes raccoon trailing and treeing, hunting voice, stamina and active alert intelligent temperament.

VBO:0201401.summary: Steady and persistent, the Weimaraner brings a strong nose and watchful attention to hunting work. It searches for game, points and follows up after the shot on land or water; its early development is closely associated with the German court of Weimar.
VBO:0201401.historicalRoots: German versatile pointing and retrieving dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 99: Weimaraner
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents Weimar court history, versatile pre- and post-shot field/water hunting, strong scenting, steady persistence and watchfulness.

VBO:0201415.summary: Alert, cheerful and self-reliant, the West Highland White Terrier keeps the courage of its Scottish hunting ancestry. Terriers from the Poltalloch area pursued quarry and controlled vermin around rough-country farms; the lively readiness to investigate remains a central part of its character.

sources.title: Royal Kennel Club: West Highland White Terrier
sources.evidence: Royal Kennel Club account traces the breed to Scottish/Poltalloch terriers and their hunting origins.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 85: West Highland White Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes alert, cheerful, courageous, self-reliant and friendly temperament.

VBO:0201424.summary: The Wire Fox Terrier is often alert, curious and fearless, yet friendly and forthcoming with people. Its quick reactions served active fox work, where a dog had to keep investigating when quarry vanished underground; that blend of nerve and sociability remains its signature.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 169: Wire Fox Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes the Wire Fox Terrier as active, alert, quick, keen, friendly, forthcoming and fearless; the breed's fox-working origin is reflected in its historical purpose.

VBO:0201435.summary: Xiasi dogs from Guizhou have long been valued locally for a keen nose, speed and courage in hunting, along with watchfulness at home. The tradition is still active: selected dogs have recently entered formal police-dog training, carrying a regional working skill into a new setting.

sources.title: Guizhou University: Guizhou Xiasi dog
sources.evidence: Guizhou agricultural biodiversity source documents the local Xiasi dog population in Guizhou.

sources.title: Kingly Xiasi dog becomes online sensation — Guizhou provincial government
sources.evidence: Provincial government account describes Xiasi hunting and home guarding, courage, scent and speed, and selection for police-dog training.
